entry.title: 292 S/4HANA tables answer one thing to ABAP and another to the database. I counted them
entry.content:
Ask an S/4HANA 2023 system how much unrestricted stock is in table MARD. With ABAP SQL, my lab says 4,860,442. With native SQL on HANA, same table, same client: 3,500.

Same system, same second. Only one of the two answers is right.

Ok, but what does this change in my day? If you write AMDP, native SQL, HANA views on the ABAP schema, or if you are connecting an AI agent straight to the database, quite a lot. So I went to my labs and counted.

Where the difference comes from

In S/4HANA many classic tables have a replacement object: a CDS view registered in DD02L, field VIEWREF. When ABAP SQL reads the table, the database interface reads the CDS view instead. MARD is redirected to NSDM_V_MARD, which calculates the stock from MATDOC. The physical MARD still has its 937 rows with the right keys, but nobody maintains the stock columns anymore.

The ABAP documentation (chapter "DDIC - Replacement Objects") lists who is NOT redirected: native SQL (ADBC, EXEC SQL), AMDP, database procedures and views, and the one I didn't expect: ABAP SQL on a CDS view that selects from such a table. In the words of the documentation, "The replacement object must be accessed directly."

SAP has its own example of that last case. FAA_ANEK_ORI is a CDS view whose whole definition is select * from anek. ABAP SQL on ANEK returns 20 rows in my 2023 lab and 197 in my 2020 lab. ABAP SQL on FAA_ANEK_ORI returns 0 in both.

How many tables are like this

One SELECT on DD02L gives the list. S/4HANA 2023 (release 758) has 292 of them, S/4HANA 2020 (release 755) has 293. 179 are transparent tables and 113 are DDIC database views. Between the two releases only 2 entered (/SCMB/GTS_MOT and /SCMB/GTS_MOTT) and 3 left, so the list is stable enough to keep in mind.

Most of them are the ones you know from the simplification list: inventory (MSEG, MKPF, MARD, MCHB, MSKA, MSLB and their history tables), material valuation (MBEW, EBEW, QBEW, OBEW), asset accounting (ANEA, ANEK, ANEP, ANLC, ANLP), CO line items (COEP) and the old ledger tables like FAGLFLEXA.

What surprised me most was the delivery class. 47 of the 292 are customizing tables. T012K, the house bank accounts, is one of them: ABAP SQL returns 10 rows in my 2023 lab, native SQL returns 198. Its replacement, V_T012K_BAM, reads FCLM_BAM_T012K_BASE from Bank Account Management, and the source has this comment from SAP: "Redirection interface for T012k. Re-generating from template required. NEVER RELEASE!!!". The EWM handling unit types in /SCWM/THUTYP are another one, with 26 rows through ABAP and 0 in the database.

The numbers

Each table counted twice in each lab, ABAP SQL first and native SQL on HANA second, always for the logon client.

TableS/4HANA 2023, ABAP / nativeS/4HANA 2020, ABAP / native
MSEG, rows1,440 / 18,394 / 0
MKPF, rows1,020 / 13,780 / 0
MARD, rows937 / 9371,064 / 1,064
MARD, sum of LABST4,860,442 / 3,500501,385,358.803 / 3,875
MBEW, sum of LBKUM4,865,306 / 0501,388,829.803 / 0
ANEK, rows20 / 0197 / 0
ANEP, rows40 / 0679 / 0
ANLC, rows68 / 01,076 / 0
COEP, rows816 / 212,995 / 32
BSIM, rows780 / 07,872 / 0
T012K, rows10 / 19816 / 61
/SCWM/THUTYP, rows26 / 07 / 2
MATDOC, rows (no replacement object)1,460 / 1,4608,397 / 8,397

Two lines in this table matter more than the big differences. MATDOC is the control: no replacement object, same count both ways. And MARD and MBEW have exactly the same number of rows both ways. If your test is "count the rows and compare", everything looks fine, and the stock is still wrong.

What I take from this

Inside ABAP, read these tables with ABAP SQL directly, not through a CDS view of your own that selects from them, and not in AMDP. If you need the data in CDS or AMDP, read the replacement object, or better a released CDS view. For stock, I_MaterialStock_2 is released in my 2023 lab.

Outside ABAP the rule is simpler: anything that reads the database directly gets the old table, and nothing warns it. That includes the AI agents many of us are building now. If your agent can run SQL on the S/4HANA schema, this list belongs in its instructions, or better, the agent should ask the application layer and not the database.

To see the list in your own system:

SELECT tabname, viewref, contflag
  FROM dd02l
  WHERE as4local = 'A'
    AND viewref  <> ' '
  INTO TABLE @DATA(lt_redirected).

All the numbers come from my S/4HANA 2020 and 2023 lab systems, so the data is demo data and your counts will be different. I didn't run an AMDP for this post: that part comes from the ABAP documentation. I also didn't check S/4HANA 2025 or the Cloud editions.

Which of these tables does your HANA-side code, or your agent, read directly today? I'd really like to know which one surprised you, so feel free to comment.

entry.title: Re: How abap2UI5 Complements RAP and Fiori Elements – Now Also as a Custom Control
entry.content:
Hi @Gayathri_S ,

thanks a lot! Honestly, for really complex UI requirements a UI5 freestyle app in JavaScript gives you the most freedom. Especially when the logic has to live in the browser, like offline support, heavy client-side interaction or a lot of device features, freestyle is the right choice.

In practice, though, the deciding factor is often not the UI but the team. Most SAP projects I see are staffed by ABAP teams who know ABAP, ATC, transports and the business data very well, and much less JavaScript, npm and the UI5 tooling. For them abap2UI5 is a great fit: they can learn it quickly and build powerful apps in the language and tools they already use. And they don’t have to maintain a second technology stack afterwards.

So the factors I would look at:

  • Where must the logic run? In the browser (offline, very rich interaction) → freestyle. On the server (business logic, data, authorizations) → abap2UI5 works well.
  • Who builds and maintains it? A JavaScript/UI5 team → freestyle. An ABAP team → abap2UI5.
  • Lifecycle: one ABAP class, transported like any other development, versus a separate frontend project with its own build and deployment.

Drawing a hard line is difficult. It depends more on the people and their experience than on the requirement itself. And it doesn’t have to be either-or: with the new custom control, a freestyle app can take over single screens or areas written in ABAP.

Best regards

entry.title: Simplified setup of Custom Document Grounding for SAP Joule for Consultants using CIAS Automation
entry.content:
This blog is co-authored by colleagues from SAP AI Factory @Samir_Rai, @Ananny_Tripathi . We have received considerable support from @HartmutStraub from AI RIG, @AnaghaDAnanth, @karthikeyan Mohanachandran and @ Rahul Jain from SAP CLE and @YihsuanLin from SAP J4C product management team.

1. Introduction

SAP Joule for Consultants is a generative AI copilot built specifically for the SAP consulting community. Grounded in over 9 terabytes of curated SAP knowledge — including 18+ million pages of SAP documentation, 100+ SAP certifications, and implementation guides — it delivers expert-level answers based on trusted SAP content.

But every consulting organization carries its own body of knowledge: internal delivery frameworks, proprietary accelerators, client-specific runbooks, architecture decisions, and hard-won lessons that simply don't exist in SAP's public content. Custom knowledge grounding is what bridges that gap — allowing you to connect Joule to your organization's curated content so it can answer not just as an SAP expert, but as your team's expert.

What Custom Knowledge Grounding Does

Custom Knowledge Grounding extends SAP Joule for Consultants with your organization’s own documents. The documents are uploaded to a data repository, indexed by SAP AI Core Document Grounding, and retrieved at runtime to ground SAP Joule for Consultants’ answers. Users get responses that combine the SAP-curated content SAP Joule for Consultants ships with and their firm’s own methodologies, policies, and delivery standards.

Configuring custom knowledge grounding manually, however, involves its own set of connected steps — setting up the right services, connecting knowledge sources, configuring trust and authorization, and ensuring everything is wired together correctly in the right sequence. Done manually, this takes considerable time and leaves room for misses and misconfiguration.

Cloud Integration Automation Service (CIAS) changes that. In this blog, we walk through how to use CIAS to automate the setup of custom knowledge grounding for SAP Joule for Consultants — end to end, in the correct order, with a guided workflow that replaces the manual overhead with a reliable, repeatable process.

2. The Role of CIAS Automation

Cloud Integration Automation service provides you a guided workflow to activate SAP cloud solutions. The guided workflow contains instructions for manual and automated tasks to enable an easy and quick integration configuration setup. The service is also used to integrate SAP Cloud solutions to on-premises solutions or other cloud solutions. It’s a free service available for the customers.

For SAP Joule for Consultants, CIAS plays a key role in simplifying activation. Instead of working across multiple tools separately — SAP BTP Cockpit, SAP Cloud Identity, SAP Central Business Configuration, and SAP for Me — and having to get the sequence right yourself, CIAS provides one guided workflow that handles these tasks end-to-end, in the correct order.

Here’s the advantage it brings compared to the manual activation:

entry.title: Re: How to determine T052-ZTAGG for BSIK/BSAK documents w...
entry.content:
Hi  @RitaZ-12345 ,

In such cases I like to search for some standard object which is performing calculation I'm looking for.

For your case, I found an example in FM FI_TERMS_OF_PAYMENT_PROPOSE:

  IF  NOT E_ZFBDT    IS INITIAL
  AND     T052-ZTAGG GT   0.
    SELECT * FROM  T052
             WHERE ZTERM EQ I_ZTERM
             AND   ZTAGG GE E_ZFBDT+6(2)
             ORDER BY PRIMARY KEY.
      EXIT.
    ENDSELECT.

This means that, if the payment terms have limit days customized (T052-ZTAGG GT 0), the system is selecting all the records with Day Limit (ZTAGG - Day of the month until which the corresponding terms are valid) higher or equal to base line date day of the month. Then, by ordering by primary key, system ensures the first entry, with lowest day limit (ZTAGG), is considered for determining the rest of the payment terms conditions.

This is just confirming what @RaymondGiuseppi had said, but with other words 🙂

I hope this helps.

BR,

Filipe

entry.title: Re: Own Application Log App
entry.content:
Hi,

I can't look into your BTP system, but I checked the release state of the application log API in an S/4HANA 2023 system. What is released for ABAP Cloud there is the read side of the API: CL_BALI_LOG_DB (LOAD_LOG, LOAD_LOGS_VIA_FILTER), CL_BALI_LOG_FILTER and the getter interfaces IF_BALI_HEADER_GETTER and IF_BALI_ITEM_GETTER. A package with ABAP for Cloud Development can only use released objects, which is what your deployment error is saying about the service you reused.

The way that stays inside the rules is a small service of your own on top of that API:

  1. A custom entity (DEFINE CUSTOM ENTITY with @ObjectModel.query.implementedBy) for the log headers, and a second one for the items if you want to drill down.
  2. A query provider class (IF_RAP_QUERY_PROVIDER) that reads through CL_BALI_LOG_DB.
  3. Service definition, an OData V4 UI binding and a Fiori elements list report on top.

The core of the query provider, reading the headers of your object:

DATA(lo_filter) = cl_bali_log_filter=>create( )->set_descriptor( object = '/NS/EXPORT' ).
DATA(lt_logs) = cl_bali_log_db=>get_instance( )->load_logs_via_filter(
                  filter           = lo_filter
                  read_only_header = abap_true ).
LOOP AT lt_logs INTO DATA(lo_log).
  DATA(lo_header) = lo_log->get_header( ).
  APPEND VALUE #( loghandle    = lo_log->get_handle( )
                  externalid   = lo_header->external_id
                  logtimestamp = lo_header->log_timestamp
                  loguser      = lo_header->log_user
                  errors       = lo_header->number_error_items ) TO lt_result.
ENDLOOP.

Around it you need the usual parts of a query provider: catch CX_BALI_RUNTIME, set the total count when io_request asks for it, and apply the paging from io_request->get_paging( ) before set_data. For the items, LOAD_LOG with the handle, then GET_ALL_ITEMS and GET_MESSAGE_TEXT on each item. If you have many logs, pass the user's filter into SET_TIME_INTERVAL and SET_MAXIMUM_LOG_NUMBER of the filter object instead of loading everything and paging in memory.

What I checked: a local class with this select method compiles in S/4HANA 2023 (syntax check only, nothing saved), and the same code with a wrong header attribute fails. I didn't build the custom entity or the app, and I didn't test it on BTP ABAP Environment, where the release state is what counts.

entry.title: UAE eInvoice: Capturing Down Payments and Prepaid Amounts
entry.content:
Overview

Down payments are common in many industries. When a customer pays a deposit upfront and then receives an invoice for the remaining balance, the UAE PINT AE eInvoice standard requires the invoice to explicitly declare the amount already paid. This is the prepaid amount field.

This post walks through the three main SAP process paths for handling down payments and explains how the prepaid amount gets captured in the XML eInvoice for each one.

The Prepaid Amount in PINT AE

In the PINT AE (Peppol International Invoice) standard adopted by the UAE, the monetary totals section of an invoice carries:

Term ID Name XML Element

IBT-112Invoice total amount with VATcbc:TaxInclusiveAmount
IBT-113Paid amountcbc:PrepaidAmount
IBT-115Amount due for paymentcbc:PayableAmount

The relationship is straightforward:

PayableAmount (IBT-115) = TaxInclusiveAmount (IBT-112) − PrepaidAmount (IBT-113)

A down payment invoice (the first document) carries the full down payment amount as its TaxInclusiveAmount with PayableAmount equal to that same amount and PrepaidAmount of zero.

The invoice references the down payment and sets PrepaidAmount equal to the down payment amount already collected, so PayableAmount reflects only the remaining balance due.

<!-- Invoice monetary totals example -->
<cac:LegalMonetaryTotal>
  <cbc:LineExtensionAmount currencyID="AED">10000.00</cbc:LineExtensionAmount>
  <cbc:TaxExclusiveAmount currencyID="AED">10000.00</cbc:TaxExclusiveAmount>
  <cbc:TaxInclusiveAmount currencyID="AED">10500.00</cbc:TaxInclusiveAmount>
  <cbc:PrepaidAmount currencyID="AED">2100.00</cbc:PrepaidAmount>
  <cbc:PayableAmount currencyID="AED">8400.00</cbc:PayableAmount>
</cac:LegalMonetaryTotal>

Scenario 1: SD Down Payment via Billing Plan

This is the fully integrated SD path. Down payments are modelled as a billing plan on the sales order, and every invoice — both the down payment request and the final delivery-based invoice — is created as a standard SD billing document.

Process Flow

VA01 | Manage Sales Orders (F1873)
Create Sales Order with Billing Plan (including Down Payment milestone)VA01 | Manage Sales Orders (F1873)
Create Down Payment Request (DP Request refers to SO and the DP Billing Plan)
VA02 | Manage Sales Orders (F1873)
Remove Billing Block on the DP Request
VF01 | Create Billing Documents (F0798)
Create Down Payment Billing Document → eDocument created (Down Payment Invoice)
VL01N | Manage Outbound Deliveries (F0867A) 
Create Outbound Delivery
VF01 | Create Billing Documents (F0798)
Create Billing Document (refers to Outbound Delivery) → eDocument created (prepaid amount captured)

How the Prepaid Amount Is Captured

When the final billing document is created in VF01 against the outbound delivery, SAP SD billing knows about the prior down payment billing document linked to the same sales order via the billing plan. The billing value calculation nets out the already-invoiced down payment amount.

The eDocument mapping reads the billing document's financial data — specifically the cleared down payment offset — and places this value into cbc:PrepaidAmount. The down payment billing document itself becomes the Down Payment Invoice eDocument (with PrepaidAmount = 0), while the final delivery invoice carries PrepaidAmount equal to the down payment value.

Key Points

  • The down payment billing document is submitted as a separate eDocument before the final invoice.
  • No FI posting is needed to trigger the prepaid amount: the entire lifecycle stays within SD billing.
  • The billing plan configuration (payment milestone type, percentages or fixed amounts) drives the down payment value.

Scenario 2: SD-FI Down Payment

In this scenario the sales order exists in SD, but the down payment is posted through the FI module directly rather than through a SD billing document. This is common when the down payment is handled by the finance department independently from the SD billing cycle.

Process Flow

VA01 | Manage Sales Orders (F1873)
Create Sales Order
F-37 | Post Down Payment Request – Customers (F1689)
Create Down Payment Request (optional; creates a noted item)
F-29 | Post Down Payment – Customers
Create Down Payment Document (optional, refers to DP Request) → eDocument created (Down Payment Invoice)
VL01N | Manage Outbound Deliveries (F0867A) 
Create Outbound Delivery
VF01 | Create Billing Documents (F0798) 
Create Billing Document (refers to Outbound Delivery) → eDocument created (should NOT be submitted yet)
F-39 | Clear Incoming Down Payments – Customers (F8969)
Clear Down Payment against the final customer invoice → eDocument updated with prepaid amount

How the Prepaid Amount Is Captured

The VF01 billing document triggers the initial creation of the eDocument, but at that moment the down payment has not yet been applied against the open receivable. The eDocument is therefore held — it should not be submitted to the tax authority at this point.

The clearing step (F-39) links the down payment posting to the open invoice item. After clearing, the eDocument framework detects the change on the underlying accounting document and updates the eDocument. The cleared down payment amount flows into cbc:PrepaidAmount, and cbc:PayableAmount is recalculated as the net amount due.

Only after F-39 is the eDocument ready for submission.

Key Points

  • The Down Payment Document from F-29 generates its own eDocument — the Down Payment Invoice submitted before the final invoice.
  • The final billing document eDocument must not be submitted before the F-39 clearing step.
  • F-39 triggers the eDocument update that populates PrepaidAmount.
  • F-37 (the DP Request) is a noted item and does not generate an eDocument on its own.

Scenario 3: FI Down Payment (No SD Sales Order)

This scenario applies to standalone financial transactions — service invoices, lease prepayments, or any situation where no SD sales order is involved. The entire lifecycle runs through FI.

Process Flow

F-37 | Post Down Payment Request – Customers (F1689)
Create Down Payment Request (optional; creates a noted item)
F-29 | Post Down Payment – Customers
Create Down Payment Document (optional, refers to DP Request) → eDocument created (Down Payment Invoice)
FB70 | Create Outgoing Invoices
Create Customer Invoice → eDocument created (should NOT be submitted yet)
F-39 | Clear Incoming Down Payments – Customers  (F8969)
Clear Down Payment against the customer invoice → eDocument updated with prepaid amount

How the Prepaid Amount Is Captured

The mechanism mirrors Scenario 2. FB70 posts the customer invoice and the eDocument framework creates an eDocument, but the document must not be submitted before clearing.

F-39 applies the previously posted down payment against the open invoice item. The eDocument is updated with the cleared amount as PrepaidAmount. The net PayableAmount reflects only the residual balance owed by the customer.

Key Points

  • F-37 creates a noted item only — no FI document, no eDocument.
  • F-29 generates the actual down payment posting and the corresponding Down Payment Invoice eDocument.
  • FB70 triggers initial eDocument creation, but submission waits for F-39.
  • F-39 is the event that finalises the PrepaidAmount on the final invoice eDocument.

Summary Comparison

 Scenario 1 (SD Billing Plan) Scenario 2 (SD-FI)Scenario 3 (FI Only)
Down Payment InvoiceVF01 billing documentF-29 postingF-29 posting
Final InvoiceVF01 billing documentVF01 billing documentFB70 posting
Prepaid Amount SourceSD billing plan nettingF-39 clearingF-39 clearing
eDocument hold required?NoYes (before F-39)Yes (before F-39)
Clearing step needed?NoF-39F-39

Submission Sequence

Regardless of scenario, the submission sequence to the UAE tax authority must always be:

  1. Down Payment Invoice eDocument — submitted first, confirms the advance payment collected.
  2. Invoice eDocument — submitted after the prepaid amount is cleared, carries PrepaidAmount and reduced PayableAmount.

Submitting the final invoice before the down payment invoice, or submitting the final invoice before the clearing step in Scenarios 2 and 3, will result in an invalid eDocument with a missing

or incorrect PrepaidAmount.

Fiori App Reference

Transaction Fiori App Name App IDVA01 Manage Sales Orders F1873VA02 Manage Sales Orders F1873VF01 Create Billing Documents F0798VL01N Manage Outbound Deliveries F0867AF-37 Post Down Payment Request – Customers F1689F-29 Post Down Payment – Customers  F-39 Clear Incoming Down Payments – Customers F8969FB70 Create Outgoing Invoices  

Confirm via the SAP Fiori Apps Reference Library.

Configuration Note

For the eDocument framework to correctly identify a billing document or FI posting as a down payment and map it to the appropriate PINT AE document type, the DRC process configuration for UAE must be active and the down payment process subtype must be correctly assigned. Verify this in the DRC Cockpit under the UAE country scope.

FI Document Type for Down Payments (Scenarios 2 and 3)

The FI document type assigned to down payment postings (F-29) must be different from the document type used for normal customer payment receipts. The eDocument framework relies on the document type to classify an incoming posting as a down payment and trigger the Down Payment Invoice eDocument. If down payment postings and regular customer payments share the same document type, the framework cannot distinguish between them — eDocuments will be created for both, causing regular customer payment receipts to incorrectly trigger eDocument generation..

Related Resources

  • PINT AE Business Rules — docs.peppol.eu/poac/ae/
  • SAP Note 3705171 — UAE e-Invoicing Implementation Overview
  • KBA 3729281 — UAE eInvoicing Programme FAQ
  • SAP Blog — What You Need to Know on the UAE DCTCE Model and the Rollout Plan

entry.title: Joule Studio Live Demo: Building a Purchase Requisition Agent in 45 Minutes
entry.content:
In our second Hackathon Alumni session, Luca Tallarita, Senior Development Consultant at SAP, took a use case submitted by community members and built an AI agent with Joule Studio. This was live and unscripted, while around 30+ participants asked questions that many early adopters are probably wondering about right now also. The timing was actually good: as the SAP TechEd 2026 Innovation News Guide puts it, "general availability for Autonomous Enterprise assistants and agents, Joule Work and Joule Studio is now underway in a phased approach." 

Context and Community

The SAP "Business meets AI" hackathons in Zurich, Munich, Berlin and Vienna brought together business and technical users to explore AI use cases on SAP BTP. After the first alumni session, where teams shared what happened after the hackathon and their use cases (see From Prototype to Practice), the community voted for a hands-on Joule Studio session as the next topic.

Quick Pulse Check: Where Does the Community Stand?

We started with a Mentimeter poll as check-in. Nobody had "never heard of" Joule Studio. Nine had heard of it, seven had already seen demos or completed e-learnings, and three were actively using the first version. That gave Luca a solid baseline to skip the basics and go deeper. And we see that the Alumni is an informed cohort. 

Purchase Requisition Creation as Use Case

Luca and his team developed a use case submission and voting app, which is a great approach to involve people and crowdsource ideas. From three submitted use cases, Luca selected a purchase requisition scenario. The challenge here was: Procurement staff spend excessive manual effort processing purchase order confirmations received via email, leading to inefficiencies and delayed updates in SAP.

A typical process that takes significant manual effort and could benefit from AI support. 
See below the screenshot from the app and the AI enhanced description.

Joule Studio's Intent-Based Development Process

Luca then walked us through the four-step process that Joule Studio follows:

1. Intent Summary

The starting point is always a business problem described in natural language, not technical specifications. Joule Studio asks clarifying questions (e.g. "Which S/4HANA deployment does your organization use?" or "Which PR creation scenarios should the agent support?") until it has a complete picture. The more detail you provide upfront, the fewer questions it asks.

There is also a "Quick Create" option that skips the clarifying questions. Joule Studio then makes assumptions based on standard processes. This is useful for speed, but the guided path produces more tailored, concreter results.

The intent file that Joule Studio generates includes the business challenge, goals and success criteria, milestones, business architecture (mapped to SAP end-to-end processes via the EKX knowledge graph), and a fit-gap analysis of available APIs and MCP servers. Below in the screenshot you see how you can chat with the intent summary to iteratively optimate the Intent.

2. Product Requirements Document (PRD)

Based on the intent, Joule Studio generates a structured PRD covering: purpose and value proposition, expected time savings and business metrics, user profiles and personas, user goals and tasks, product principles, scope definition (in/out), and a prioritized list of requirements (must have, high want, nice to have, non-functional). It also includes a solution architecture recommendation with an overview of the architecture, integration points, etc. 

3. Specifications

The specification is the technical bridge between requirements and code. It contains step-by-step instructions for the coding agent: guidelines for the agent framework (Python), skill definitions, MCP server configurations, and dependency management. This step is primarily relevant for developers who want to review or adjust the technical approach. The good thing is, that you also can check the source codes and edit them for example. 

4. Build Solution

After confirming the specification, you tell Joule Studio to build. In Luca's case, the coding phase took roughly 15 minutes. Joule Studio generates the agent code, creates MCP servers for each required API (translating SAP APIs into MCP format), writes test cases, and iterates until tests pass. 

The result is a complete asset folder with an AI agent and multiple MCP servers, ready for preview and deployment.

The Preview enables interacting with the Agent

Joule Studio includes a preview mode where you can interact with the generated agent using mock data. Luca asked the agent "What can you do for me?" and it listed three capabilities: creating a purchase requisition from a framework agreement, from a catalogue item, or as a free text order.

 

He then tested it with "Create a PR for a new MacBook" and the agent walked through the process, checking framework agreements and catalogue items. With real system integration, the agent would pull live data from S/4HANA and Ariba.

Deployment, Versioning and Collaboration

Additional capabilities Luca demonstrated were:

  • Deployment: One-click deployment from Joule Studio into an SAP-managed sub-account. Each MCP server and the agent are deployed separately and can be reused by other agents.
  • Git integration: Connect to GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. Joule Studio pushes changes to the repository, and you can pull local changes back. You can also download asset files as a zip for offline development.
  • Versioning: Full lifecycle management with version history and the ability to roll back to earlier versions.
  • Collaboration: Add colleagues as viewers or editors to work on the same solution.
  • Monitoring: Analytics and monitoring dashboards for deployed assets.

Luca is a senior technical consultant and so to say early adopter and poweruser of Joule Studio. While he is not from product management we managed to answer most of the following questions.

FAQ: Questions from the Community around Joule Studio

The session generated many questions. Here are the answers as discussed:

Can Joule Studio connect to S/4HANA (public or private cloud)? Yes. If you have your own Joule Studio instance, it can access your systems. The demo ran on an internal staging environment without external system access, but the generated code prepares the integration. The final connection steps may need manual configuration.

Can you connect Joule Studio to GitHub? Yes. GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket are supported. Joule Studio pushes changes to the repository, and you can push local changes back.

Is MCP connectivity for external tools planned? MCP connectivity to SAP tools is available. Re Connectivity to external (non-SAP) MCP tools you may check the official documentation (or ask Joule for Consultants :-).

How is Joule Studio activated? Is it a BTP service? Joule Studio is entitled through the SAP for Me portal. A dedicated sub-account is created and SAP-managed. It is not activated like a regular BTP service.

What are the prerequisites? A BTP global account is the main prerequisite. LeanIX and Signavio integration is optional but obviously improves results, as Joule Studio can then scan your actual processes and system landscape.

Can you upload custom process descriptions or templates? Not as templates directly, but you can edit the generated files (intent, PRD, specifications) and paste your own content. With LeanIX and Signavio in place, your process descriptions feed into the generation automatically.

Are standard SAP processes sufficient without Signavio? Joule Studio knows standard SAP processes through the EKX knowledge graph. Without customer-specific process documentation via Signavio, it uses standard processes as the default. Results are more accurate with Signavio, but it is not required.

What is the relationship between the previous Joule Studio and the current version? They are different products. The skill creation from the previous version is now one option among many in the current Joule Studio (available under the "Extensions" tab). RE migration path you might also check the official documentation. (one thing i find also noteworthy: the previous version was not pro-code).

How are custom skills handled? Custom skills can be created in the Extensions area of Joule Studio. Of course you can build them also just via Claude for example. However if you want to build Skills in the SAP context, Joule studio has much more SAP context and thus is a much better option.

How are authorizations handled? The generated MCP servers do not include technical user configuration. Authorization management for system access is still a separate step. Governance of deployed applications is handled in the SAP-managed account.

Can I include custom OData APIs? Joule Studio knows published SAP APIs from the API Hub. For custom APIs, you need to provide the information manually in the intent or PRD. Joule Studio will include it in the build process but cannot discover custom APIs automatically.

Can the agent be integrated into other AI chatbots like Copilot? The agent is A2A (agent-to-agent) enabled and accessible via an endpoint URL. It can communicate with other agents that support the A2A protocol. The specific integration steps depend on the target environment.

How does deployment work? What about integration with SAP Work Zone? After deployment, the agent is available behind an endpoint URL. It can be integrated into Joule Work or other agent landscapes via A2A. The specific Work Zone integration path was not demonstrated in this session.

What about pricing and early adopter care? For early adopter questions, contact your dedicated program manager through the Early Adopter Care program. For pricing, please contact your sales contacts at SAP.

Reflections: 400 Use Cases and Counting

Sascha Faller highlighted the team behind Joule Studio: young, engaged developers who consistently demonstrate the tool live at events, under pressure, with real customer use cases. Luca shared that his team has been at 34 events so far, with 24 more planned, and has built 400 use cases with Joule Studio. As Luca put it: "When we started in May, we ourselves saw progress and improvements in the tool really rapidly. I think now we're at a stage where it's really fast, it really gets great results."

Luca's personal reflection on the tool's value: developers already have the technical skills to automate repetitive work, but business users often lack the technical capability to do so. Joule Studio bridges that gap. A business user can describe a challenge, and Joule Studio builds a working prototype. This also improves collaboration between business and technical teams: the business describes the problem, Joule Studio creates a prototype, and the technical team understands exactly what needs to be built.

In his experience, the learning curve is steep. First-timers can create agents with it, and the process itself is straightforward once you understand the chat-based interaction pattern.

Community Feedback: The Word Cloud

The closing Mentimeter asked participants to describe their impression of Joule Studio in one word. From 10 responses: exciting (2x), promising, collaborative, the future, fast, efficient, guiding, wow, and "not so easy as it looks." A mix of optimism and realism that reflects well where the product and the market stands as it enters the phased general availability.

We will also try to get some experiences from the AI Agent Hackathons in November & December. If you want to present your AI journey or current challenges, please reach out. And if you are an early adopter in the SAP AI world and want to join the community - please also feel free to reach out.

entry.title: What's New in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608.3: Two Manufacturing Innovations Worth Knowing

The latest feature delivery collection for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition - release 2608.3 (HFC6) - brings targeted but meaningful enhancements to manufacturing operations. While not a major release, these two updates address real day-to-day pain points for production planners and shop floor teams. Here is a closer look at what has changed and why it matters.

Controlled Routing Changes Are Now a Reality

 
For anyone working with discrete manufacturing, routing accuracy is non-negotiable. A routing defines how a product is made - the sequence of operations, work centers, and processing times. Until now, making changes to an existing routing in the Manage Routings app lacked the governance layer that many regulated and quality-conscious industries demand.
With this update, that gap is closed. When you select Edit with Change Number from the Change dropdown in the Manage Routings app, you are prompted to enter a change number before the Change Routing app even opens.
 
Manage Routings - Edit with Change Number
 
Every modification made in that session is then recorded under that change number, creating a clear, auditable trail of who changed what and when.

 

This is more than a convenience feature. For industries where engineering change management is a compliance requirement - think automotive, aerospace, pharmaceuticals - having routing changes tied to a formal change number is the difference between a controlled process and an uncontrolled one. It also makes it far easier to trace back the origin of a production issue if a routing was recently modified.
 
The feature is part of scope item BJ5 (Make-to-Stock Production for Discrete Manufacturing) and requires the Manage Routings app (F5425) to be assigned to the relevant business users.

Manufacturing Order Printing Gets the Flexibility It Always Needed

 
The second enhancement tackles a limitation that has challenged manufacturing teams for a long time: the rigid, one-size-fits-all approach to printing documents for manufacturing orders.
 
Previously, when a manufacturing order was released, its documents printed automatically. Full stop. That default behavior works fine in some scenarios, but it does not reflect how many real production environments actually operate.
 
Some processes need shop floor papers at a different stage of the order lifecycle. Others should not print automatically at all - perhaps because a digital workflow handles the handover, or because unnecessary printouts are simply waste.
 
SAP has now introduced two new output modes alongside the existing default:
 
Flexible Printing of Manufacturing Orders with Output Determination

 

  • Output Control-Based: Rather than triggering automatically on release, printing is governed by your Output Determination (OPD) rules. You define the logic; the system follows it. New decision-table columns have been added for the order's output mode and eight order statuses (including Confirmed), giving you precise control over when documents are generated.
  • Manual: No automatic printing at all. Documents are printed on demand, by a user who actively requests them.
Importantly, nothing breaks on upgrade. Every existing order type retains the original Automatic on Release behavior until you explicitly change it. The new modes are configured per plant and per order type, meaning you can run different printing behaviors side by side within the same system - which is exactly what organizations with diverse production processes need.
 
To activate a new mode, navigate to your configuration environment and open either Define Order-Type-Dependent Parameters for Production Orders: 
 
Define Order-Type-Dependent Parameters for Production Orders

 

or Define Order-Type-Dependent Parameters for Process Orders: 
 
Define Order-Type-Dependent Parameters for Process Orders

 

From there, choose the Output Mode on the Implementation tab: 
 
In the Implementation Tab: Output ModeThis feature covers both discrete manufacturing (scope item BJ5) and process manufacturing based on process orders (scope item BJ8), so it is broadly applicable across production environments.

The Bigger Picture

 
Both features share a common theme: giving manufacturing teams more control and visibility. Whether that means tracing a routing change back to a specific change number, or aligning document output with the actual milestones of your production process rather than a single system event, the direction of travel is clear. SAP continues to bring the governance and flexibility that enterprise manufacturing demands into the cloud.

entry.title: Re: SAP HANA access through MCP: recommended architecture...
entry.content: @israelsturaro thanks, now it's clearer. For the workload part I looked at what HANA itself offers, in my S/4HANA 2023 lab (HANA 2.00.073), because that is where an MCP server with a database user lands. 1. Yes, it can be managed, and HANA has the tool for it: workload classes and workload mappings. A class can set STATEMENT_TIMEOUT, STATEMENT_MEMORY_LIMIT, STATEMENT_THREAD_LIMIT, the same limits as totals for all statements of the class, a PRIORITY, and admission control thresholds that queue or reject statements above a CPU or memory level. A mapping puts sessions into a class by USER_NAME, APPLICATION_NAME, CLIENT and a few more. For your setup that means a dedicated database user for the MCP server, one workload class with a timeout, memory and thread limits and a low priority, and a mapping on that user. In my lab all of this is at default: statement_memory_limit is -1 and default_statement_concurrency_limit is 0, so no limit, and the only workload class is SAP's own, for the statistics user. Nothing stops a heavy generated query until you configure it. Rate limits and fixed query patterns in the MCP server are still worth having on top, because the database can only stop a query that is already running. 2. OData or ABAP services run on the same HANA, so they don't remove the load. What they change: requests go through the ABAP work processes, which is a natural limit on concurrency, the queries are the ones the service defines, and the database knows who is asking. In my lab the 36 sessions from the ABAP server all carried APPLICATION, APPLICATIONUSER (the SAP user) and APPLICATIONSOURCE (program and line) in M_SESSION_CONTEXT, and a workload mapping can match APPLICATION_USER_NAME and APPLICATION_SOURCE. So you can also limit one service or one business user without a separate database user. 3 and 4. For analytics at volume, a separate copy is the clean way to protect the transactional system, and the isolation only comes from replication. A federated or remote access sends each query back to the source, so the load stays where it was. I haven't tested Datasphere for this, so take this part as architecture advice, not a measurement. What I measured: the columns of WORKLOAD_CLASSES and WORKLOAD_MAPPINGS, the memory and concurrency parameters, and the session context in the 2023 lab. I didn't create a workload class or run a load test.

entry.title: Finding Success During Implementation and Adoption
entry.content:
Finding Success During Implementation and Adoption

Lessons from Sumeet Kulshrestha on turning procurement technology into sustainable business value

💡A procurement transformation can reach go-live and still fall short of its promise. In this episode of The Future of Procurement Podcast, Sumeet Kulshrestha, VP, Delivery - Finance & Spend Management (FSM) at SAP, draws on more than two decades in procurement services to explain why implementation success depends on more than technology. His message is practical: organizations create value when they connect business ownership, governance, adoption, integrations, and continuous improvement from the start.

Go-live is the starting line, not the finish line

🚦One of the most important reframes in the discussion is that go-live should not be treated as the destination. The real transformation begins when people start using the system; transactions begin flowing, and the organization learns whether new processes work across procurement, finance, accounts payable, HR, and other connected functions. Sumeet notes that many challenges surface after deployment, which makes ongoing attention to adoption and value realization essential.

🌱That changes how leaders should think about implementation. A launch is not a one-time technology event. It is the start of a sustained operating model in which processes evolve, people change roles, organizations acquire businesses, and new capabilities become available. The companies that keep "watering the plant" are better positioned to continuously improve rather than freezing their transformation at the moment of go-live.

Fit to standard, then customize with purpose

🧭 Cloud solutions have changed the customization equation. In the on-premise era, organizations could modify core code so extensively that upgrades became difficult. Today, cloud platforms create stronger boundaries. That makes a fit-to-standard mindset valuable, but it does not mean every configuration or customization is harmful.

⚙️The sharper question is why a deviation is needed. Customizing technology simply to reproduce an old process can preserve complexity instead of removing it. But a targeted change that supports a meaningful business outcome can become a source of innovation. Sumeet points to invoicing against a contract as an example of a customer-created capability that ultimately informed broader product innovation. The test is whether the change is scalable, outcome-driven, and worth the long-term operational cost.

Procurement transformation is an enterprise transformation

🔗Procurement does not operate on an island. Sourcing, buying, contracting, invoicing, supplier processes, and external workforce activities connect to systems and teams across the enterprise. A procurement deployment that overlooks those dependencies can create friction elsewhere, even if the procurement design itself appears sound.

👥This is why business involvement matters so much. The strongest projects put knowledgeable stakeholders at the table early and give them enough capacity and authority to make decisions. Rather than asking IT to push a solution into the business, organizations need procurement, finance, AP, HR, IT, and other affected groups to shape how the new operating model will work together.

Governance turns debate into decisions

🛠️ Projects can also stall when ownership is unclear and every decision is pursued through consensus. Effective governance needs named decisionmakers, regular cadence, clear agenda items, and the authority to resolve trade-offs. Implementation partners add more value when they present genuinely distinct options and explain the consequences, rather than transferring a long menu of choices back to the customer.

🎯For adoption, Sumeet favors pragmatic rollout strategies over unnecessary big-bang risk. Start with receptive users or a manageable group, prove that the process works, learn from real behavior, and expand. In some cases, pairing enthusiastic users with demanding stakeholders can expose weaknesses early while still creating advocates for the change.

When something feels wrong, act early

🚨The most expensive solution is one an organization buys but does not use. If adoption is weak, value is not materializing, or the implementation feels off-course, waiting only compounds the problem. Sumeet recommends asking for help early and using an honest health assessment to understand where outcomes are being lost.

📈His recovery model is straightforward: assess, stabilize, and optimize. First, identify the root causes across technology, process, integration, governance, and adoption. Next, stabilize the operating environment and decision model. Then optimize the outcomes that justified the investment in the first place. Asking for help is not a sign of failure. It is evidence that leaders are serious about protecting the business case.

AI expands the toolkit, but people still matter

🤖AI will increasingly handle repeatable work and add new capabilities to procurement, but Sumeet does not see it eliminating the human dimension of transformation. Judgment, context, governance, and connection to customers remain central. In that sense, the familiar three-legged stool of people, process, and technology may gain another leg: AI, governed deliberately and used to extend what teams can accomplish.

✅The takeaway is simple: procurement transformations do not fail because they encounter speed bumps. They fail when organizations stop steering. Success comes from treating the implementation as an enterprise change, making decisions with discipline, staying close to users after go-live, and intervening early when value starts to drift.

Take the next step

💭Reflection: Where is your organization treating go-live as the end of the journey, and what governance, adoption, or integration issue deserves attention now?

entry.title: Re: Request SAP clarification on the standard date determ...
entry.content:
Hi,

The date the delivery due list selects on is not the confirmed delivery date. In RVV50R10C the "Delivery Creation Date" on the selection screen is declared as SELECT-OPTIONS st_ledat FOR vepvg-ledat (include V50RSEL_LEDAT), so it is compared with LEDAT in the SD delivery due index VEPVG. LEDAT is filled when the sales order is saved, in function group V05I, include LV05IF0V, FORM INDEX_VEPVG_AUFBAUEN:

IF lvbep-tddat > lvbep-mbdat.
  ledat = lvbep-mbdat.
ELSE.
  ledat = lvbep-tddat.
ENDIF.

So LEDAT is the earlier of the material availability date (MBDAT) and the transportation planning date (TDDAT) of the schedule line. The same FORM then keeps the earliest of these dates per shipping point, route, forwarding agent, ship-to party and goods issue date, and FORM LEDAT_SETZEN (include LV05IFDA) writes it into VEPVG-LEDAT. The confirmed delivery date (EDATU) is not used, and the goods issue date (WADAT) only takes part as a key of the index.

I checked it against the data in two labs. In S/4HANA 2023, VEPVG-LEDAT is equal to the earlier of MBDAT and TDDAT of the confirmed schedule line in 94 of 94 index rows, and equal to the confirmed delivery date in only 72 of 94. In S/4HANA 2020 it is 58 of 58, against 5 of 58 for the confirmed date.

That explains your Tuesday deliveries. Backward scheduling starts from the confirmed delivery date and subtracts transit time, loading time, transportation lead time and pick/pack time, in working days of the calendars. A Tuesday delivery with two or three days of lead time gets MBDAT or TDDAT on Friday or Monday, and a Friday run with Current Date +0 to +3 selects Friday to Monday, so the order is due. This is the standard design: the due list shows when the delivery has to be started to arrive on time, not when the customer receives it.

To confirm it in your system for one order, compare MBDAT, TDDAT, WADAT and EDATU of the schedule lines in VBEP with VEPVG-LEDAT for the same VBELN in SE16. If LEDAT is the earlier of MBDAT and TDDAT, the selection is working as designed, and what you would change is the scheduling data (route transit time, loading and pick/pack times, factory calendars) or the date range of the variant, not the program. If you really need another rule, SAP lists the user exits of the due list in include V50R_USEREXITS, two of them for the selection screen.

What I didn't test: ZSTD standing orders and route schedules, and a run of RVV50R10C with your variant. I read the code in S/4HANA 2023 only. The change markers in that FORM are from release 3.0, so I expect the same logic in ECC, but I didn't check it there.

For your SAP HCM / HR consulting work, you can also use general-purpose AI assistants to help interpret ABAP code, understand HR infotypes and payroll concepts, troubleshoot errors, draft functional specifications, and prepare test scenarios. Always validate the answers against your ECC release, applicable SAP Notes, and client-specific configuration.

entry.title: Re: Upload GL journals with 999+ line items with park/app...
entry.content:
Hi,

I looked at this in the code of my S/4HANA 2023 lab, and the workflow part also in 2020, because the answers to your first and third questions are in the Fiori posting logic itself.

1. Parking more than 999 lines without summarization: not in standard. The parked document tables keep the 3-digit item number: BUZEI is NUMC 3 in VBSEGS, VBSEGK, VBSEGD and VBSEGA, the same as in BSEG, while ACDOCA-DOCLN is CHAR 6. The BSEG bypass you found is the posting status BSTAT = 'U' ("Posting in General Ledger Only"), and CL_FDC_POSTING_IMPL refuses to park it with message FDC_POSTING_001 155 "No document parking permitted for posting status &" (foreign currency valuation is the only exception). The comment above that check says it directly: for an upload with BSTAT = 'U' but less than 999 line items, upload again with BSTAT space.

3. Workflow for a document parked with BAPI_ACC_DOCUMENT_POST: the decision is in CL_FDC_ACCDOC_VER_SERVICES, method IS_DOC_VALID_FOR_NEW_WORKFLOW. A document is relevant for the verification workflow when its transaction code is FBDC_P001 (the posting service of the Fiori apps, FAC_GL_DOCUMENT_POST_SRV), the foreign currency valuation one, or, in 2023, the supplier down payment request. Documents from the accounting interface (AWTYP BKPFF) are accepted only in the cloud edition (the check is CL_COS_UTILITIES=>IS_S4H_CLOUD). The branch for external documents on premise is in the method, commented out, with the note "this is currently not enabled", in 2020 and in 2023. On top of that the document must be parked as complete and only G/L and supplier lines are allowed (account types 'SK'). The list of the app follows the same rule: I_GLJrnlEntryToBeVerified only selects parked documents with TCODE FBDC_P001, FBDC_P050 or FBDC_P051. So a document parked by the BAPI gets a different TCODE, never shows up in Verify General Journal Entries, and no workflow starts. The released RAP business object I_JournalEntryTP (C1, ABAP Cloud) doesn't help here either: it has Post, Change, Reverse and Validate, but no park action.

2. That leaves the split. What the standard supports is several documents of up to 999 lines, each one parked and verified on its own, so the approver gets one work item per document. I didn't check whether the upload of Verify General Journal Entries has an extension point to do the split for you, so I can't confirm that part. If one approval for the whole journal is a hard requirement, that would be your own approval step before posting with the 999+ upload, and that is custom.

What I measured: the field lengths in the DDIC, the code of the three classes and the CDS view, and the message texts. I didn't run the apps, upload a file with more than 999 lines, park through the BAPI or test Public Cloud.

entry.title: HANA Integrated LiveCache Migration using SUM Homogeneous DMO
entry.content:
Migrating SAP systems to RISE is an important step toward improving system performance, simplifying the IT landscape, and preparing for digital transformation. One of the specialized scenarios in this process is HANA Integrated LiveCache Migration using SUM Homogeneous Database Migration Option (DMO), which involves migrating an SAP system along with its integrated LiveCache components to SAP HANA while maintaining system consistency and minimizing operational disruption.

The Database Migration Option (DMO) of Software Update Manager (SUM) combines system update activities with database migration, providing a streamlined approach to moving an SAP system from a supported source database to SAP HANA. In scenarios involving SAP APO or other applications that use LiveCache functionality, additional planning and technical considerations are required to ensure that LiveCache objects, data, and dependencies are handled correctly during the migration.

This blog explores the key concepts, prerequisites, preparation activities, migration approach, and important considerations involved in performing a HANA Integrated LiveCache Migration using Homogeneous DMO. It also highlights the areas that require special attention during execution, helping SAP Basis administrators and migration consultants better understand the process and prepare for a successful migration.

It is very important that we migrate the HANA LiveCache data successfully during migration.

Reason:

SUM will asks whether the LiveCache migration should be done Automatically (Taken care by SUM) or Manually (Taken care by consultant)

Selecting Automatically Scenario:

We used Automatically as this has many errors going forward in SUM.

Here, SUM run the report /SAPAPO/OM_LC_DOWNLOAD_UPLOAD at preprocessing phase just before entering the downtime (After Preparation for Downtime phase)

This report performs the consistency check and download the report. The consistency check should be passed and the download of LiveCache data takes place, this should be successful otherwise SUM will throw the error and would not be able to move forward.

And if we successfully pass the download LiveCache data in pre processing. The SUM will again try to Upload the downloaded LiveCache data in Postprocessing phase.

This will end up with an error as the report will run the consistency check in target system this will end up with error.

Note: You can skip this error by following the instruction in this SAP note 2562164.

Solution and helpful suggestion:

Choose manual execution of LiveCache report so that we can manually download and upload the LiveCache data.

You can use the new report i.e., /SAPAPO/OM_LC_DOWNLOAD_UPLOAD2

This report does not validate the consistency check of LiveCache.

During pre processing SUM will provide you the screen for downloading the LiveCache data.

Logon to the system and execute the report /SAPAPO/OM_LC_DOWNLOAD_UPLOAD2

Make sure the section A is performed and the table is empty before downloading the LiveCache data

Above image has data we are going to clear that.

Click on “Delete Download Table and Logs” to delete the previously downloaded Livecache data so that we can freshly download.

The above image is after deleting the previously downloaded data (Section A)

Now, click on “Download LiveCache Data” in section B. This will download the LiveCache data into a table.

You can see the number of entries in the table. The name of the table is /SAPAPO/OMDWNUPL (Just for validation purpose)

After this step of downloading the LiveCache data kindly proceed forward with the SUM downtime.

Now, in SUM Post Processing Phase

SUM will stop and ask to upload the downloaded live cache data on target system.

Login to the target system and execute the report /SAPAPO/OM_LC_DOWNLOAD_UPLOAD2

The screen will look something like this before upload on target.

Now, kindly select option on section C: Upload Upload LiveCacheData

After successfully uploading the LiveCache data the screen will look something like below.

Note: Please do not click anything in section A and section B. In target system we should only select section C: Upload

After this we can proceed with the SUM. This completes the successful migration of LiveCache data from source to target.

The downloaded data will be in database. We should run this report and upload the LiveCache data from the database to the HANA LiveCache and this is our responsibility.

Thank You,
Ranjith R

RISE with SAP SCM APO SAP LiveCache software logistics toolset

entry.title: Re: SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud – Are New G/L Accounts Autom...
entry.content:
Hi,

Short answer from the code: yes, a G/L account created in the system itself is added to the hierarchies whose range covers it, without editing and saving the hierarchy again. I checked it in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, which is on premise but uses the same Manage Global Hierarchies runtime, so keep the release difference in mind.

Why something has to do it: the range only exists in the design time of the hierarchy (a node with a range sign and a low and high value). The runtime that the reports read, HRRP_NODE and HRRP_NODE_N, has one leaf per account and no range field at all. In my lab the FSV hierarchies have 53,126 leaf nodes. So a new account needs its own leaf.

What does it: the G/L account master has the BAdI GL_ACCOUNT_MASTER_REPLICATE, and SAP's implementation FINS_FI_GLACC_HRRP_REPLICATION (class CL_FINS_HRRP_GLACC_REP_BADIIMP) calls function module HRRP_GL_ACCOUNT_DELTA with the chart of accounts, the account and the action. For an insert it updates the OB58 FSVs and the Manage Global Hierarchies FSVs, and then runs a generic delta (CL_FINS_UH_HRRP_DELTA_UPDATE) that looks for range nodes where the account is between the low and the high value and creates the leaf in the runtime tables. In dialog the function module runs as a background task after the save, so the account shows up a moment later, not in the same second.

About KBA 3587911: an account that arrives by transport is written by the import and doesn't go through the G/L account save, so this BAdI doesn't run for it. That is my reading of the code and it fits the KBA. The same function module also has a cloud branch: when the system is cloud and the Q2P transport is active, it transports the affected FSV and hierarchy versions after the update.

What I measured: the runtime tables, the BAdI implementation, the function module and the delta class in the 2023 lab. I didn't create an account to watch it happen, and I didn't test Public Cloud 2602 or the transport case of the KBA.

entry.title: Re: Parallel crcy area (crcy type 40) missing for area 01...
entry.content:
Hi,

You already found the cause. The long text of ACC_AA 116 says it directly: the parallel currencies of the leading ledger and the depreciation areas in Asset Accounting must be the same. Company code 830 has currency type 40 (hard currency) and 030 doesn't, so CDCN never needed an area for type 40, and the copy CD83 doesn't have one either.

That leaves two ways:

  • If 830 really needs the hard currency, add a parallel currency area for type 40 to CD83 and then assign the chart.
  • If type 40 in 830 came from the copy and nobody needs it, remove it from the currency settings of 830 instead. Decide this before the first postings in 830.

How the area should look: SAP's sample chart 0CL in my S/4HANA 2023 lab already has one. Area 01 Book deprec. posts in real time, and area 50 "Hard curr." has currency type 40 (field CURTP in T093A), takes the values from 01 (Adoption of Values from Depreciation Area = 01), takes the depreciation terms from 01 (Dep. Terms Transfer = 01) and is set to "Area Does Not Post". That is exactly what the long text asks: the parallel currency area must have the same settings as the posting area, and the only difference is that it doesn't post. The sample charts 0AR, 0CO, 0MX, 0PE and 0VE also have type 40 areas if you want to compare.

In the IMG of Asset Accounting the steps are: Determine Depreciation Areas (create the new area in CD83, copying 01), Specify Transfer of APC Values and Specify Transfer of Depreciation Terms (both from 01), and Specify the Use of Parallel Currencies (type 40 for the new area). Then try the assignment of CD83 to 830 again.

What I measured: the message and its long text, T093 and T093A of the sample charts, and the names of the IMG activities, all in my S/4HANA 2023 lab. I didn't build the area in a chart and assign it to a company code, so try it in a sandbox first.

entry.title: Re: File attachments at header level of requisitions
entry.content:
Hello,

Thank you very much for your question.

Here is the AI-generated response. Please check whether it helps you resolve the issue.

Kind regards,

Henrike

Header Attachments for Purchase Requisitions via Workflow

Header attachments are supported for purchase requisitions in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, but support depends on the application, release, attachment framework, and point in the process. Header attachment enablement was delivered for Public Edition in release 2302 through the attachment facet.[1] However, the My Purchase Requisitions app still supports attachment creation only at item level.[2]

Workflow limitation

Standard flexible workflow does not provide an activity for an approver to upload a new attachment to the purchase requisition header during approval. The workflow inbox primarily displays attachments already linked to the business object. Therefore, calling API_CV_ATTACHMENT_SRV from workflow custom logic should not be treated as a supported method unless the API metadata for your tenant explicitly exposes the purchase-requisition header as a supported business object and permits creation.

This is distinct from private-edition functionality: from SAP S/4HANA 2025, My Inbox can display existing purchase-requisition header attachments, but that feature applies to SAP S/4HANA and SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, not Public Edition.[3]

Standard options

  1. Add the attachment before workflow submission

    • Use Manage Purchase Requisitions – Professional or Create Purchase Requisition – Advanced, depending on the process and release.
    • For newer releases supporting header DMS attachments, add the document through the header Documents/Attachment area rather than the GOS-style attachment list.
    • In release 2602, external DMS document type SL1 can be added at PR header level and can subsequently flow to the purchase order.[4]

  2. Configure Harmonized Document Management

    • In configuration activity/SSCUI 105346 – Activate HDM for Attachment Object Type, activate:
      • PURCHASEREQUISITION
      • PURCHASEREQUISITIONITEM
      • PURCHASEORDER, if PR-to-PO transfer is required.
    • Activate the DMS framework and maintain the applicable default document type:
      • SL1 – external use
      • SL9 – internal use.[4]
    • Ensure the business role contains authorization to change PR attachments; the relevant standard catalogs include SAP_MM_BC_PR_PROCESS_MC and SAP_MM_BC_SSPPR_MANAGE_PC.

  3. Use item-level attachments where self-service requisitioning is required

    • Item-level attachments remain the standard supported approach in My Purchase Requisitions.[2]
    • This is generally the safest option when approvers must see documents associated with individual approval items.

  4. Side-by-side extension

    • If the attachment must be collected during approval, implement a separate SAP Build Process Automation or SAP BTP application to collect and store the document.
    • Link it to the PR through a supported released API only after confirming that the target release exposes header-level attachment creation for the PR object.
    • Do not rely on an undocumented business-object type or internal object key with API_CV_ATTACHMENT_SRV, because this is not a stable, supported Public Cloud extension pattern.
Important distinction

GOS and DMS attachments behave differently. GOS attachments are assigned to one business object and are not transferred automatically from PR header to PO header; SAP supports item-level transfer when both objects use DMS attachments.[5] For release 2602, the supported header transfer path uses DMS/HDM and requires documents to be uploaded in the header Documents area, not through the GOS attachment list.[4]

Recommendation: If your tenant is on 2602 or later, use the standard HDM/DMS header configuration and require the requester or purchaser to attach the document before submitting the PR. If your release or application does not expose that header capability, use item-level attachments or a side-by-side document-collection process. Adding a PR header attachment directly from an approval step is not a standard flexible-workflow capability.

Batch Printing Correspondence

For journal entries, use Create Correspondence (F0744A) with correspondence type SAP09 Internal Document and select either Entry View or Ledger View. For supplier-invoice correspondence, the standard process may remain document-specific; for example, complaint-letter output is opened and printed from an individual supplier invoice.[6] If no suitable mass-output app exists for the required correspondence type, consider a side-by-side extension using released APIs, or submit a feature request through SAP Customer Influence.[1]

SAP S/4HANA Cloud: Mass Update BP SSF Communication Type

Use the full BusinessPartnerTemplate generated by your tenant, not the example file. Example files are illustrative and may omit optional fields; the full template contains all fields supported by the current system. The import app can generate either an example file or a full system-specific template.[1]

For the SSF column:

  • Enter X to activate SSF as the business partner’s communication type.
  • Leave it blank if SSF should not be selected.
  • Do not enter the text SSF.
  • Retain the BP key and all mandatory technical/key columns from the generated template.

For existing business partners:

  1. Export the affected records with Export Master Data – Business Partners.
  2. Keep the exported structure unchanged and populate SSF with X.
  3. Upload it using Import Master Data – Business Partners (F6553A, successor to the former Import Data for Consolidation app).[2]
  4. Run the consolidation process and validate a small test set before processing all BPs.

If the SSF value represents a new subordinate record rather than an update to an existing BP record, unhide _ACTION_CODE and enter uppercase I. SAP specifies that new rows are inserted through file upload using an action code; updates to existing values normally do not require it.[3] [4]

If SSF = X is rejected during validation, do not try alternate values blindly. Confirm the field tooltip/value help in the generated template and raise an SAP support incident for the BP mass-processing component, because field availability and accepted operations can vary by release.

SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud: Recurring Journal Entries at Scale

A supported standard mass-creation option for recurring journal entry templates does not currently exist in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition. SAP confirms that F1598 has no mass-upload function and that no API is available for creating recurring journal entries in bulk.[1] An Excel upload for recurring templates is likewise unavailable.[2]

A. Mass creation of recurring journal entries
  • F1598 supports creating and saving individual recurring entries, including their line items and recurrence rules.[3]
  • The recurring entry is only a template; scheduled processing later creates the actual journal entries.[4]
  • There is no supported bulk-create mechanism for these templates in Public Edition.[1]
  • Do not build against FAC_RECURRING_ACCOUNTING_DOC_SRV unless SAP explicitly lists and releases it for your Public Edition release. The technical information available for that service identifies support for SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition rather than Public Edition.[4]
B. Mass upload of recurring templates

There is no standard spreadsheet, CSV, migration object, or released interface for uploading recurring-entry templates in Public Edition.[1] [2]

The Upload General Journal Entries app, F2548, can import multiple ordinary journal entries from XLSX or CSV and post them, but it uploads actual general journal entries—not recurring templates or recurrence rules.[5] [6]

C. Supported alternatives

  1. Upload each period’s actual journals with F2548

    Generate the period’s journal-entry file externally and upload it through F2548. The app supports multiple entries per file, error correction using the original batch ID, verification, and posting.[5]

    This is generally appropriate when:

    • periodic amounts or account assignments can change;
    • business users want spreadsheet-based control;
    • the volume is manageable as a controlled file upload.

  2. Post actual journals through the released Journal Entry API

    For high-volume or unattended processing, generate each period’s due postings outside the recurring-template framework and send them through a released Journal Entry Post API. SAP identifies synchronous and asynchronous bulk SOAP interfaces for remote journal posting, with the bulk interface intended for larger workloads.[7] SAP guidance also identifies journal-entry APIs as suitable for large transaction volumes.[8]

    This automates actual journal creation, not creation of F1598 recurring templates.

  3. Use a clean-core side-by-side solution on SAP BTP

    A scalable pattern is to maintain schedules and template data in a side-by-side application, calculate the due postings, validate accounting objects, and call only released SAP APIs. Similar implementations use SAP Integration Suite for inbound orchestration and SAP BTP for mappings, transformations, and posting generation.[9] [10] This approach supports tailored business rules without compromising SAP S/4HANA upgrade stability.

  4. Assess process-specific automation

    If the entries represent accruals, deferrals, allocations, leases, or another defined accounting process, assess the relevant standard process automation rather than reproducing everything as generic recurring journals. F1598 is most suitable where posting keys, accounts, and amounts remain fixed.[4]

D. Recommended scalable approach

Use the following decision model:

  • Small, stable template population: Create templates manually in F1598, use copy where practical, and run the standard recurring-posting process.
  • Large population with periodic file preparation: Generate actual postings externally and use F2548.
  • Large, repeatable, unattended volume: Store schedules outside F1598, generate due journals on SAP BTP or another governed integration layer, and post through a released journal-entry API.
  • One-time opening balance or cutover requirement: Use the applicable migration object for balances or open items, not recurring-template migration. Migration and operational journal posting are separate use cases.[8]

For the BTP/API option, include:

  1. A governed schedule and template store.
  2. Company-code, currency, account-assignment, and balancing validations.
  3. Idempotency keys to prevent duplicate postings.
  4. Simulation or approval before posting where required.
  5. Batching and API payload-size controls.
  6. Error staging, correction, and reprocessing.
  7. Posting-result reconciliation and audit logging.
  8. Monitoring and notifications for failed runs.
Conclusion

Your assessment is correct: F1598 cannot mass-upload recurring journal entry templates in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, and there is currently no released recurring-entry creation API for that purpose.[1] The supported scalable alternative is to automate the resulting periodic journal entries through F2548 or a released Journal Entry Post API, preferably using a clean-core SAP BTP side-by-side design for high-volume requirements.[5] [7] If native recurring-template mass creation remains mandatory, the appropriate route is to support the published SAP feature request referenced in the relevant SAP KBA.[1]

No. SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition 2608 does not provide standard output functionality that automatically sends an approved Service Entry Sheet (SES) to the supplier by email or generates a printable SES PDF.

Troubleshooting: Credit Memo Tax Dates

This behavior is generally standard because SAP treats a credit memo as a correction invoice rather than as a normal invoice.

  • Credit memo with reference to an original invoice: The Tax Fulfilment Date is derived from the original invoice’s Tax Fulfilment Date. The Tax Reporting Date is normally derived from the credit memo’s billing date. Therefore, the Service Rendered Date entered in VF01 is not necessarily used.[1]
  • Credit memo without reference: The Tax Fulfilment Date is derived from the Service Rendered Date, while the Tax Reporting Date follows the correction-invoice rule and is normally the credit memo billing date.[1]
  • For normal invoices, the Tax Fulfilment Date is generally the Service Rendered Date and the Tax Reporting Date equals the Tax Fulfilment Date, which explains the different result you observe.[1]
  • The SD-to-FI transfer executes user exit EXIT_SAPLV60B_008 to determine these two tax dates.
Can the VF01 Service Rendered Date be transferred?

Yes, but the appropriate method depends on the deployment and country localization:

  1. SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition for Poland
    Use configuration activity Transfer VAT Date from Credit Memo to Journal Entry (SSCUI 105418). It permits selection of either the Service Rendered Date or Billing Date as the VAT date.[2]

  2. On-premise or private-edition systems
    Review the implementation of EXIT_SAPLV60B_008. SAP provides sample logic in SAP Note 3004838; any adjustment must comply with the applicable country-specific tax rules.[1]

  3. FI VAT-date framework
    Check whether VAT-date functionality is active for the company code and review enhancement spot VATDATE_RULES, BAdI VATDATE_VALUES, and the relevant implementation. This framework determines and validates BKPF-VATDATE, including documents originating from VF01.[3]

Recommended checks
  1. Determine whether the credit memo references the original invoice.
  2. Compare the original invoice’s Tax Fulfilment Date with the credit memo’s resulting date.
  3. Verify the credit memo billing type and copy-control path used for its creation; credit memos can follow separate source-document and transfer logic.[4]
  4. Debug EXIT_SAPLV60B_008 during release to accounting and check whether localization or custom code overwrites the VF01 Service Rendered Date.[1]
  5. Confirm the required date logic with the local tax team before changing it, because the standard correction-invoice behavior reflects legal reporting rules.

entry.content:
#AI-Generated Content

Our internal AI tool has provided the following response. Please check whether it helps you resolve the issue.

Kind regards,

Henrike

SAP Group Reporting: HGB Goodwill Amortization

Yes. A workaround exists in SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, and SAP Asset Accounting is generally not the appropriate mechanism for it.

SAP’s recommended Group Reporting approach is:

  1. Use activity-based consolidation of investments with goodwill in local currency.
  2. Post the amortization amount to the statistical FS item $GW_IMP for each amortization period.
  3. Let the consolidation-of-investments task generate the corresponding goodwill reduction and expense postings.
  4. To avoid entering $GW_IMP manually every period, implement the reclassification-task approach described in the attachment GW_scheduled_amortization.pdf to SAP Note 2813262. SAP states that this approach is usable from release OP2025 and that Public Cloud systems receive all applicable features.[1]

Public Edition already supports goodwill calculation in local currency and subsequent currency-translation-reserve adjustments.[2] Manual impairment adjustments are supported for the goodwill-in-local-currency methods, with the subsequent consolidation postings generated by activity-based consolidation of investments.[3]

Asset Accounting should not be used as the primary solution because consolidated goodwill is Group Reporting data rather than an operational fixed asset. Routing it through Asset Accounting would introduce unnecessary accounting-to-consolidation mappings, ledger considerations, and reconciliation requirements. It could also mix legal-entity depreciation with a group-level consolidation adjustment.

The practical design is therefore to keep the process entirely within Group Reporting:

  • Store the amortization basis and useful-life logic in dedicated statistical FS items.
  • Use reclassification rules to calculate or supply the periodic $GW_IMP amount.
  • Run the reclassification before the activity-based consolidation-of-investments task.
  • Add validation rules to prevent amortization beyond the remaining goodwill balance.
  • Test acquisition-year prorating, subsequent capitalization, ownership changes, disposals, currency translation, reversals, and balance carryforward.

For rule-based consolidation of investments, goodwill itself is manually calculated and posted because the underlying records do not contain the required parent partner unit.[4] If this is your current method, assess whether activity-based consolidation with goodwill in local currency is a better foundation for the HGB process.
